Argentina's Superintendencia de Riesgos del Trabajo (SRT) supervises the insurance that covers
registered workers against work accidents and occupational diseases, and publishes statistics on
every case that insurers notify. This notebook uses SRT's historical series from 1996: national
figures by sector, and rates by province, sex, age, size of employer and detailed sector. Read the
module [README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)

base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/main/modules/ar-srt-work-accidents/data"
read_module <- function(folder, name, ...) {
  local <- file.path("..", "data", folder, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(base, folder, name), show_col_types = FALSE,
           ...)
}

national <- read_module("tidy", "national.csv")
provinces <- read_module("tidy", "by_jurisdiction.csv")
sex_age <- read_module("tidy", "by_sex_age.csv")
size <- read_module("tidy", "by_size.csv")
sector3 <- read_module("tidy", "by_sector_3digit.csv")

# National totals for workplaces (employers in the private and public sectors)
totals <- national |> filter(sector == "Total", scope == "Workplaces")
```

**All cases** include commuting accidents and relapses; **work accidents and occupational
diseases** (AT and EP) do not. Rates count cases with days off work or a disabling injury.

# Part 1. Thirty years of work accidents

```{r long-view}
totals |>
  filter(measure %in% c("Cases per 1,000 workers", "Deaths per million workers")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = case_type)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_y") +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Workplaces covered by the occupational risk system", x = NULL, y = NULL,
       colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Questions**

1. How much did the rate of cases and the death rate fall between 1997 and 2025? Which fell more?
2. What happened in 2020, and why would you leave it out when describing the long-term trend?
3. Give three reasons, other than safer work, why reported rates might fall over 30 years.

**Your answer:**



# Part 2. Commuting accidents

```{r commuting}
totals |>
  filter(measure == "Deaths", year >= 1997) |>
  select(year, case_type, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = case_type, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(commuting_and_relapses = `All cases` - `Work accidents and occupational diseases`,
         share = round(commuting_and_relapses / `All cases`, 2)) |>
  filter(year %in% c(1997, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2025))
```

**Questions**

1. What share of the deaths of covered workers are not work accidents or occupational diseases?
   Has the share changed?
2. Argentina compensates commuting accidents as work-related. Many countries, and many statistics
   such as the EU's ESAW, leave them out. What are the arguments on each side? Who can prevent a
   commuting accident?

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. Sectors

```{r sectors}
national |>
  filter(year == 2024, scope == "Workplaces", case_type == "Work accidents and occupational diseases",
         measure %in% c("Cases per 1,000 workers", "Deaths per million workers"),
         !sector %in% c("Total", "No data")) |>
  select(sector, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  arrange(desc(`Deaths per million workers`)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 1)))
```

**Questions**

1. Which sectors have the highest death rates, and which the highest rates of cases? Are they the
   same sectors? Why might they differ?
2. Name the main hazards behind deaths in the sector with the highest death rate.

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. Provinces

```{r provinces}
provinces |>
  filter(year == 2024, sector == "Total", scope == "Workplaces",
         case_type == "Work accidents and occupational diseases", jurisdiction != "Total") |>
  select(jurisdiction, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  ggplot(aes(`Cases per 1,000 workers`, `Deaths per million workers`, label = jurisdiction)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(size = 2.5, vjust = -0.6) +
  labs(title = "Work accidents and occupational diseases by province, 2024", x = "Cases per 1,000 workers",
       y = "Deaths per million workers")
```

**Questions**

1. Which provinces have the highest death rates? Do they also have high rates of non-fatal cases?
2. Provinces differ in their mix of industries. How could you check whether a province's high death
   rate is explained by its industries? (Hint: `by_jurisdiction.csv` also has rates by sector.)

# Part 5. Sex and age

```{r sex-age}
sex_age |>
  filter(year == 2024, scope == "Workplaces", case_type == "All cases",
         measure == "Cases per 1,000 workers", age_group != "Total") |>
  ggplot(aes(age_group, value, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Cases per 1,000 workers by sex and age, 2024", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which age group of men has the highest rate? How do men's and women's rates change with age?
2. Suggest reasons, both about work and about reporting, why young men have the highest rates.
